kp.k: Survey captures experienced leaders’ expectations, not measured AI effects
kp.d: The authors contacted over 200 law firm leaders with 7 questions and received 73 detailed responses from firms with 200 to over 2000 lawyers. Of respondents, 75% had held leadership positions for over 7 years and 47% represented firms with over 500 lawyers. Additional written comments explored four strategic issues. The evidence principally concerns leaders’ priorities and expectations for 2026 rather than measured operational outcomes.
qs: we reached out to over 200 Law Firm Leaders with a series of 7 questions and were pleased to receive 73 detailed responses, representing firms ranging in size from 200 to over 2000 lawyers.
Of those responding, 75% were from Firm Leaders who had served in their Leadership positions for over 7 years and 47% were representative of larger law firms of over 500 lawyers in size

kp.k: Market uncertainty coexists with optimism about individual firms
kp.d: Respondents supplied three market descriptors: 63% selected terms grouped as uncertain or unstable, 49% challenging or competitive, and 22% positive descriptors. These groupings are not mutually exclusive. Nevertheless, 78% expected 2026 to be highly successful for their own firms.
qs: The dominant choice identified by 63% of these Law Firm Leaders was “Uncertain” and “Unstable.”
These terms were the preferred choice of another 49% of all Firm Leaders participating.
But all those positive labeled only accounted for a mere 22% of our total responses received.
we heard from 78% of our law firm leaders that they fully expect that 2026 will be a highly successful year for their firms.

kp.k: AI dominates leaders’ most compelling business concerns
kp.d: Asked about the most compelling business issue besides profitability and growth, 62% of leaders supplied technology and AI responses irrespective of firm size. Concerns span responsible delivery, associate development, hiring, pricing, client expectations, technology selection and recovering substantial investment costs. Private equity’s challenge to existing business models and the war for talent were the other leading categories.
qs: We were provided with a range of responses from 62% of all Firm Leaders, and irrespective of Firm size
Effectively incorporating AI into the legal practice while adjusting the business impact AI will have on hiring, pricing and client expectations;
Managing client expectations for the impact of GenAI to significantly reduce legal fees;
The integration of AI into law firm operations and how to pass the costs of that substantial investment on to clients;

kp.k: AI integration targets workflows, efficiencies and fewer human hours
kp.d: For 2026, the survey identifies streamlining routine legal workflow, improving internal efficiency and reducing human task hours as priorities across firms. Most leaders favor early technology adoption without necessarily being first. These are intended uses, not demonstrated productivity gains. Among firms with over 800 lawyers, moving from hourly billing toward value-based pricing overshadowed other AI integration priorities.
qs: Streamline routine legal workflow
Drive internal efficiencies
Reduce the overall number of human hours required to complete legal tasks.
there was one common issue that overshadowed all others and that was: “to shift away from hourly billing toward value-based pricing.”

kp.k: Partner retention remains the leading economic priority
kp.d: Keeping desired partners was the top economic issue across firm sizes. Business development and cultivating future rainmakers followed overall, with an emphasis on premium rather than low-value work. For firms with over 800 lawyers, innovation and AI-enabled client experience followed retention. The authors cite an unspecified report that more than a fifth of laterals leave after year three and more than a third after year five, with each failed lateral costing more than $4 million; these are reported external figures, not survey findings.
qs: Keeping the partners we want to keep.
more than a fifth of laterals leave after year three, and more than a third after year five, with each failed lateral costing firms more than $4 million.
These firms want to attract premium work in a manner that resonates with their clients and has them referring the firm to other prospects.
Using AI to improve the client experience.

kp.k: Leadership development and strategic execution constrain organizational change
kp.d: Developing market-leading practice or industry groups and client teams ranked first among leadership priorities, followed by grooming future leaders. Executing strategy ranked second among firms with over 800 lawyers. The authors connect execution concerns to their separate 2024 strategic-planning research: 69.8% spent at least three months developing a plan, only 35% had group-level plans, only 14% of the over-500-attorney group had such plans, and 18.6% reported implementing almost all their last plan.
qs: Developing market leading practice / industry groups and client teams.
Identifying and grooming future leaders.
Executing on our strategic plan while stressing the negative consequences of inertia and resisting change.
69.8% of all firms invest on average, at least three months in the development of a formal written strategic plan

kp.k: MSOs separate legal delivery from investor-backed operational services
kp.d: The authors describe growing private equity investment in management service organizations, which take over administration, accounting, technology, recruiting, HR and real estate for a fee while the law firm retains client-facing legal services. They present competing arguments: MSOs are ordinary vendors versus their operational entanglement makes interference with lawyer-client relationships unrealistic to exclude. A respondent states that MSO investors need not be licensed lawyers and financing can include debt and equity; the document does not establish a definitive regulatory resolution.
qs: The MSO is paid a fee for providing these services.
The pro-MSO argument is that they are simply vendors, no different than the outside messenger services that most law firms employ.

The counter argument is that MSOs are so entwined with the day-to-day management of the firm that it is simply not realistic to believe that they are not interfering with the lawyer/client relationships of the firm.
Investors in the MSO need not be licensed members of the legal profession. Financial structures for MSOs are deal specific and can include both debt and equity.

kp.k: Outside capital promises investment capacity but threatens professional control
kp.d: Anonymous leaders disagree about private equity. Supporters see MSOs and capital gains as ways to finance rising AI and technology costs, align partner incentives, support long-term investment and facilitate retirement succession. Critics fear profit-driven commercialization and loss of operational control. One respondent says partners distributing all profits leaves insufficient technology capital; another reports curiosity about MSOs but unwillingness to surrender control. These are attributed assessments rather than verified investment outcomes.
qs: Mergers and devices such as MSOs are seen as solutions to these challenges. Currently, we are curious but our partners are not ready to give up control of our operations and competitive edge.
Partners should be allowed to realize a capital gain if they contribute to creating value.
I worry that the third-party investment will turn law firms into purely profit-driven, commercial enterprises and mark an end to the ideal of law firms as professional organizations.

I believe our industry operates with an obsolete business model: where partners distribute all profits among themselves, and there is no capital left to invest in technology nor financial incentives for them to stay, creating structural volatility that will prevent competition in the next decade.

kp.k: Private equity requires partner alignment and explicit exit planning
kp.d: One leader advises obtaining 100% buy-in across partner levels, suggesting some firms need at least 2 years to prepare finances and agreement. That respondent describes a 5-year investor exit requiring a 10–15-year success plan and retention of experienced management and partners. Another, discussing an article, stresses that investors’ expected exit, timing and consequences must be understood because PE ownership permanently changes a firm. These are recommendations and expectations, not survey-wide findings.
qs: Some firms will need at least 2 years to get that kind of buy in and present their finances properly.
PE is not a short term-term endeavor as they are looking for a 5yr-exit; but to sell the stake there needs to be a 10-15yr plan and a path to success.

In the PE world, exit (with a profit) is everything, so everyone involved needs to be very clear on how that’s envisioned, when it’s expected to occur, and what will happen to the business when that day comes.

kp.k: Litigation funding combines affordability opportunities with independence concerns
kp.d: The authors predict litigation funders will accelerate nonlawyer investment in 2026. They quote a US Chamber of Commerce report by Skadden lawyers dated August 29, 2024 alleging funder control threatens lawyers’ independence and loyalty. Respondents acknowledge ethical risks but also opportunities to finance meritorious claims, including high-stakes IP disputes. One firm reports limited early use, conditioned on suitable funders and terms, with appeal arrangements, law firm time investment and success returns requiring analysis.
qs: In 2026, litigation funders will play a key role in accelerating the pace of nonlawyer investment in law firms.

Private Equity funders exercise significant control over litigation, contrary to their claims of being passive investors. This control threatens the professional independence of lawyers, and disrupts the loyalty that counsel owe to their clients.
I can imagine certain situations, especially on the plaintiffs’ side, where litigation funding allows meritorious actions to be brought.
Our experience is too new and few to make final determinations, but we are certainly looking at and using it where it makes sense.

kp.k: Authors predict continued hallucination incidents and delayed measurable ROI
kp.d: The authors assert that court sanctions have not stopped increasing AI misuse and predict the problem will continue through 2026. Separately, they claim corporate legal departments are adopting AI faster than firms but will not achieve measurable ROI in 2026 because adoption and data readiness remain uneven. They describe systems, baselines and consistent use as prerequisites for measurement and client demands as pressure on firms to catch up. No quantified incident series or ROI study accompanies these assertions.
qs: But the problem continues to increase and will do so throughout 2026.
Meanwhile, corporate legal departments are rapidly adopting AI, but 2026 will not bring about a measurable Return On Investment . . . yet.
The issue isn’t failed technology, it’s uneven adoption and weak data readiness.
Legal teams are still building the systems, baselines, and consistency needed to measure AI’s impact, making 2026 a foundational year.

kp.k: Leaders disagree about AI capabilities and lawyer employment
kp.d: Anonymous comments range from broad skepticism about LLM capability to predictions of transformation across service delivery, organizational structures, education, hiring and pricing. One leader expects efficiency gains and changed work rather than necessarily fewer lawyers, arguing that growing complexity and law increase demand even as technology takes over some complex tasks. The document therefore presents disagreement, not a consensus employment forecast.
qs: The issue is, LLM is simply the wrong model. It just can’t do what it’s sold to do.
I don’t think that means fewer lawyers; I think the work of lawyers is going to change.
But I have no doubt that this is a technology that will have a major impact on the business model of law firms.

Its adoption will change everything – the delivery of legal services, the structure of law firms and in-house legal departments, the training of young lawyers, the pricing model, legal education, the hiring of new lawyers, etc.

kp.k: Junior training pathways face predicted disruption
kp.d: Associate training appears both as a survey concern and as a sharper prediction in follow-up comments. One respondent predicts AI will eliminate junior training jobs and require firms to bear training costs directly. Another claims AI is taking entry-level jobs and questions how younger workers will begin careers. These comments are predictions and perceptions, without supporting legal employment measurements in the document.
qs: Providing training & development of young associates in the context of AI;
AI will eliminate junior training jobs and force firms to assume training costs like any modern industry.
AI is taking entry-level jobs. What happens when Gen-Zers can’t start their careers?

kp.k: Strategic business advice remains central to lawyer value
kp.d: A respondent argues that clients need business decisions informed by legal knowledge rather than statements of law, and regards this as a longstanding skill that remains valuable with or without technology. Another expects AI to make the distinction between pure legal analysis and strategic business advice more important. The source presents this as a competence and service-value argument, not a measured shift in task allocation.
qs: Clients aren’t looking to be told what the law says; what they need is business advice, based on legal knowledge, that aligns with their interests.
For the best lawyers, these skills will be the same with or without technology.
The specialist redefines what it means to be a great lawyer: moving from pure legal analysis to strategic business advice, a distinction that AI will make even more critical.

kp.k: AI efficiency could undermine hourly billing economics
kp.d: Respondents predict AI will accelerate fixed, project-based and value-based pricing by reducing the hours underlying existing economics. One expects firms themselves to press clients to abandon hourly billing; another advocates charging for outputs rather than inputs. The authors suggest, more speculatively, that 2026 may see AFAs overtake hourly billing as CLO demands intensify. Their assertion that Europe and Asia have embraced AFAs while North America remains hour-dependent is not accompanied by comparative figures.
qs: 2026 may be the year that AFAs take over from the billable hour and rate pressures reach a breaking point.
The price will shift from charging for input — the hours we dedicate to the client — to charging for output to the client.

For the first time ever, law firms will press clients to move away from the billable hour in favor of project-based billing, because the basis for the billable hour (leverage/hours x billable rates) will erode quickly.

kp.k: AFAs require scope management and may retain hourly monitoring
kp.d: One leader expects AI, improved scope estimation, prompt handling of scope changes, project management and knowledge management to enable more predictable budgets. That leader qualifies the move away from hours by noting clients still want to monitor hours and rates underlying AFA outcomes. Another attributes AFA pressure to elite Big Law partner rates exceeding $2,000 per hour and midsize firms’ difficulty raising rates, arguing alternative pricing can address demands for transparency, technology-enabled services and speed.
qs: Big Law is commanding rates exceeding $2,000 per hour for elite partners, while midsize firms struggle to raise rates.
we will increase our ability to deliver predictable budgeted outcomes, which is something we all want.
I would note that many clients still wish to monitor the hours and rates that go into our AFA outcomes.

kp.k: One leader predicts broader access and midsize-firm disappearance
kp.d: An anonymous respondent predicts AI will accelerate value-based billing and mass access to legal services while eliminating midsize firms that try to serve everyone. This is a sweeping individual forecast, without supporting market data or a specified mechanism for reaching people with unmet civil legal needs.
qs: AI will accelerate the transition to value-based billing and mass access to legal services. Mid-sized firms trying to be all things to all people will disappear.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The authors and anonymous firm leaders predict changes to legal workflows, pricing, staffing, training and competition, while expressing materially different views about AI’s capabilities and its effect on lawyer numbers.
pts.d: McKenna and Rynowecer report that 62% of surveyed leaders identified technology, specifically AI, as a compelling business issue. Respondents anticipate effects on hiring, pricing, associate development, client expectations and firm economics. For 2026, surveyed firms intend to streamline routine workflows, improve internal efficiency and reduce human hours; these are reported priorities, not demonstrated productivity results. Among firms with more than 800 lawyers, moving from hourly billing to value-based pricing overshadowed other AI-integration priorities. The authors predict that court incidents involving AI hallucinations will continue increasing despite deterrence and sanctions. They also assert that corporate legal departments are adopting AI rapidly, but will not achieve measurable ROI in 2026 because adoption is uneven and data readiness and measurement systems remain inadequate. They describe law firms as lagging corporate departments and facing client demands to close the technological-competence gap. Anonymous leaders offer divergent assessments: one expects greater efficiency and major business-model change without necessarily fewer lawyers, because legal and worldly complexity increase demand; another says LLMs cannot do what they are sold to do and distinguishes human anticipation from machine capabilities; another predicts transformation of service delivery, organizational structures, training, education, pricing and hiring. One leader reports firing a client over AI-generated material and claims AI is taking entry-level jobs; a separate leader predicts elimination of junior training jobs and firms having to bear training costs themselves. On professional value, one leader sees business advice grounded in law as an enduring skill unaffected by technology, while another argues AI will make the distinction between legal analysis and strategic business advice more important. On pricing, the authors suggest AFAs could displace hourly billing in 2026. Leaders predict AI will accelerate fixed-fee and value-based billing, erode the hours-based revenue foundation and cause firms themselves to push project billing. Other leaders expect improved scope estimation and predictable budgets, competitive disadvantage for non-adopters, wider access to legal services and the disappearance of generalist midsized firms. These are separate attributed views rather than a unanimous forecast.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers a survey of leaders and qualitative follow-up testimony, rather than measured AI performance, productivity, employment or ROI results.
pts.d: The authors contacted over 200 firm leaders with seven questions and received 73 detailed responses from firms of 200 to over 2,000 lawyers. Of respondents, 75% had held leadership positions for over seven years and 47% represented firms exceeding 500 lawyers. The 62% figure measures the salience of technology/AI as a business concern, not AI adoption or realized gains. The authors subsequently solicited written views and held one-on-one discussions about four strategic issues; the number of follow-up participants is not supplied. AI workflow and billing priorities are survey findings, whereas broader transformation, displacement and competitive forecasts are anonymous respondents’ judgments. The authors refer generally to court filings containing hallucinations and monetary sanctions but identify no cases or incident counts supporting their projected increase. Their assertions about corporate adoption, lagging firms, absent measurable ROI and data readiness are not accompanied by adoption statistics or ROI studies. The entry-level employment concern includes a leader’s firsthand report of terminating a client relationship over AI material, plus a broad assertion that CEOs are laying off 20–30% of workers; no dataset, sample or causal analysis is supplied for that percentage. The skeptical leader invokes unnamed experts and autonomous-driving analogies, not legal-AI tests. Predictions about demand, training costs, pricing, access and midsized firms rest on professional opinion and proposed business mechanisms. Another leader’s budget-predictability claim attributes improvement jointly to AI, scope management, technology, project management and knowledge management. No benchmark results or measured hallucination rates are provided.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The main horizon is 2026, but many leader predictions are open-ended and qualified; the document preserves both rapid-change expectations and skepticism.
pts.d: Published in 2025, the report explicitly frames AI integration plans, continuing hallucination incidents, foundational ROI work and client pressure on firms around 2026. The authors’ statement that AFAs may take over in 2026 is tentative, not a definite prediction. Their ROI claim concerns measurability during that year and attributes the limitation to uneven adoption, weak data readiness and missing systems and baselines, rather than technological failure. Most leaders specify no date for transformation, junior-job elimination, wider access or generalist midsized-firm disappearance. One anticipates rapid erosion of hourly-billing economics; another describes fixed-fee growth and hourly inefficiency disappearing gradually. The no-necessary-reduction-in-lawyers view is qualified by growing complexity and expanding law, alongside acknowledgment that technology already handles some complex work. The continuity view claims that business-advisory skills have mattered for 40 years and will still matter 40 years hence. The optimistic budget forecast depends on advances beyond AI alone and notes that some clients will continue monitoring hours and rates under AFAs. Firm leaders also describe product selection and monetizing AI investment as unresolved challenges. In the adjacent financing discussion, a leader links rising AI and technology costs to interest in mergers and MSOs, but says that leader’s partners are not ready to surrender operational control.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims principally concern medium-to-large law firms and corporate legal buyers, with additional predictions about junior careers, courts and wider public access.
pts.d: Law firms across the surveyed size range face intended reductions in task hours, AI investment and cost-recovery challenges, changes to hiring and pricing, and client pressure for lower fees and technological competence. Firms exceeding 800 lawyers particularly emphasize value-based pricing and improving client experience. Partners and firm leaders face threats to hours-based economics, strategic product-selection decisions and pressure to finance technology; one leader identifies AI costs among reasons AmLaw firms consider mergers and MSOs. Corporate legal departments are described as faster adopters but still building the foundations for measurable returns, and as subject to organizational transformation. Clients are portrayed as demanding thoughtful adoption, reduced fees, transparent pricing, faster turnaround and business advice rather than legal exposition alone. Junior lawyers and entrants face predicted loss of training jobs, altered hiring and education, with firms assuming training expenses; the separate concern about Gen Z and 20–30% workforce cuts extends beyond legal employment and should not be read as a measured lawyer-job-loss claim. Practicing lawyers may shift toward strategic business advice rather than simply decline in number. Courts encounter continued fabricated material in filings and enforcement burdens. Generalist midsized firms are singled out by one respondent as vulnerable to disappearance, while another predicts non-adopting firms will fall behind. The statement about mass access to legal services concerns wider service availability but does not identify underserved populations or quantify a reduction in unmet civil legal need.
